posts.author: Cherry
posts.body:
ATT_Turan said:
There's no such thing as plugins for RPG Maker 2003. As several people mentioned above, 2k3 does take any kind of scripting and has to have patches that alter the actual executable.
Click to expand...
There is such a thing - for DynRPG, which however is not compatible with the official version of RPG Maker 2003 as of now.
Additionally, there are patches (for both legacy and official versions).
People sometimes confuse the terminology here, especially because patches in IPS format could also be dropped into a special folder if DynRPG was used, much like its actual plugins.
To summarize:
* Plugins (in the form of DLL files for DynRPG) are currently not supported with the official RM2k3 version. (The same goes for "quickpatches" in the form of a line of text like  "SomethingSomething=123ABC,45,678DEF,9A".)
* Patches (in the form of IPS files) are supported
as long as explicitly stated that they work with the official version (1.10+) or with 1.09a+
. Trying to use an incompatible patch will usually destroy your game engine (possibly in a way not immediately noticeable), so always create a backup of RPG_RT.exe before testing patches. Note that for some patches, multiple versions were released (sometimes by different people). Make sure to pick the right version for your engine (it should be compatible with 1.12a, possibly written as something like "1.10+", etc.)
* Patches distributed as binaries (EXE files) to overwrite your RPG_RT.exe with should not be used with the official version either, because it may result in a downgrade which will cause incompatibilities with your RPG Maker version.
The term "add-on", albeit rarely used, would encompass all kind of extension or modification of the engine. You could also call everything listed above a "mod" of some kind.
Marcello8z said:
Question: how to (in RPG MAKER 2003) make a animated tile such as water or grass?
Click to expand...
Please ask questions separately, don't hijack the existing thread with a new, unrelated question. Anyway, the answer is to look at how the existing tilesets do it and do the same. You can also read a description of the tileset format in the
help file
(the rightmost button in your toolbar), under "Material Reference" => "Tileset Specification". There, check out blocks A1, A2 and B for animated water that also creates shorelines automatically, or blocks C1, C2 and C3 for other general-purpose animated tiles. You can also use events to place animated objects on a map. To gain more animated tiles or to do more complicated animations on commonly-used tiles (which would be cumbersome to do as events because they would be all over the map), some games use a common event that utilizes the "Change Tile" event command to swap all instances of a certain tile on the map with another one, resulting in an animation when done periodically.
